summary: This unit teaches you to give safe, neat braiding services: consult with the client and check her scalp and hair, prepare natural hair, choose extension hair, braid cornrows (cane rows), box braids and twists with the right tension, finish the ends safely, and give aftercare and removal advice. It also covers preventing traction alopecia, hygiene, comfort and posture, and records.

blocks.p: Braiding is one of the most popular services in Jamaican salons and one of the oldest hair skills in the African diaspora. This unit covers the whole service, from the first conversation with the client to the day her braids come out. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

A braided style can last for weeks and sits on the scalp the whole time, so mistakes show and hurt. Braids that are too tight cause pain, bumps and hair loss. Braids put in over a scalp problem can spread it. That is why this unit is about **tension, scalp checks and judgement** as much as neat hands.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: a full head of straight-back cornrows on natural hair, and box braids with extensions with the ends sealed safely. The assessor watches your consultation, preparation, partings, tension, hygiene and records, not only the finished style.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, your hands and the work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A braiding service can take many hours, and you work close to the client's scalp with sharp tools, hot water and long pieces of loose hair. Safe habits protect both of you.

blocks.h: Hazards and how you prevent them

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Scissors and the tail-comb tip
Cuts and stabs
Cut away from the skin and close scissors after each cut
Never leave scissors open on a client's lap or in a pocket
Hold the tail comb pointing away from the face and eyes
Hot water for sealing synthetic ends
Scalds to the client or to you
Keep the container on a steady, low surface away from the client
Dip the ends away from the skin, then lift them out with care
Never carry hot water past a seated client
A flame or lighter near synthetic hair
Burns; fire; melted fibre on skin
Use the method the Centre allows; hot water is safer
Never use a flame near the client's scalp or hair
Keep a fire extinguisher where you can reach it
Loose hair and extension pieces on the floor
Slips and tangles around your feet
Sweep up often during a long service
Keep a bin beside you
Long sitting and bending
Back, neck, shoulder and wrist pain for you; stiffness and numb legs for the client
Adjust the chair height so that you do not stoop
Change your position and stretch; take short breaks
Offer the client breaks and a comfortable chair with her feet supported
Dirty tools and hands
Passing on germs and scalp infections
Wash your hands before each client
Clean, then disinfect combs and clips for every client
Use a clean towel, cape and neck strip
Heat from a hairdryer used to stretch the hair
Scalp burns; dry, damaged hair
Use a comb nozzle and heat protectant; keep the dryer moving
Use low to medium heat

blocks.note: For a burn or scald, cool the area at once under cool running water for about 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or oil. Cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing and get medical help for anything more than a small red area. Tell your instructor and write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Cleaning** removes hair and product with detergent and water. **Disinfecting** then kills most germs on the clean tool, for the contact time on the label. Cleaning always comes first.
Every client has clean, disinfected combs and clips. A tool that falls on the floor is cleaned and disinfected before it is used again.
Never use a comb that has hair on it. Remove the hair, wash, rinse, soak in disinfectant for the full time, rinse if the label says, dry and store covered.
Fresh towel, cape and neck strip for every client. Used ones go into a closed laundry bin.
Keep extension hair in its packet or a clean, closed box, off the floor. Do not reuse extension hair from one client on another.
Do not braid over a scalp with lice, ringworm or sores. After such a client, bag the towels for a hot wash and disinfect everything she touched.
Wash your hands after the service and after touching your phone.

blocks.note: Never photograph or post a client's scalp or face without her agreement. Keep client details private, as the Data Protection Act requires.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Braids are made by crossing three strands of hair over or under each other. Twists use two strands wound round each other. Knowing the names and what each does helps you advise the client.

head: Style
What it is
Notes
rows: Cornrows (cane rows)

Three-strand braids made flat against the scalp along a parting, picking up hair as you go. The strands cross **under** the middle one (underhand), so the braid sits raised on top. In Jamaica they are often called cane rows.
Straight back, curved, or in a pattern. A good base for wigs and weaves. Little hair is left free.
Feed-in cornrows
Cornrows where extension hair is added in small pieces as the row goes along.
Less pull at the start than putting all the extension in at once; gives a natural, tapered look.
French (overhand) braid
Strands cross **over** the middle one, so the braid lies on top of the hair, while hair is picked up from both sides.
A smooth braid lying on the head; not the usual choice for natural, coily hair.
Box braids
Single braids, each from its own square parting, with or without extensions. They hang free from the scalp.
Many sizes; the size depends on the hair strength and the look wanted.
Knotless braids
Box braids that start with the client's own hair, adding extension hair a little at a time, so there is no knot at the root.
Less weight and pull at the root; often feels lighter and more comfortable.
Two-strand twist
Two strands wound round each other to the ends.
A gentle style on natural hair; the ends can be curled or sealed.
Flat twist
A two-strand twist made flat on the scalp, picking up hair as it goes.
Often used to set up a twist-out or a style.
Senegalese or passion-type twists
Two-strand twists made with extension hair.
Long, rope-like twists; the extension weight matters.
Fishtail braid
A braid made from two sections, crossing small pieces from the outside of one section to the other.
A decorative finish.
Micro braids
Very small box braids.
Many hours of work; can be too heavy and tight for fragile hair.

head: Client
Better choice
Why
rows: Fine or fragile natural hair, or thinning edges
Larger, lighter braids or twists; a lighter extension; knotless braids
Small, heavy braids pull the hair out at the root.
A child
Simple, light, loose cornrows or twists; low tension
A child's scalp is tender and her hair is fine; heavy styles and beads cause damage and pain.
A client who swims or exercises often
A style that can be washed and dried quickly; light braids or cornrows
Heavy, damp braids can smell and grow mildew.
A client who wants a style for a short time
Two-strand twists or flat twists
They are easier to take out and can be re-done.
A client with a lot of natural hair length and strength
Box braids or knotless braids of medium size
The hair can hold the weight.

head: Type
What it is
Good points
Take care
rows: Synthetic braiding hair
Man-made fibre, sold in packs. Many types are pre-stretched.
Cheap, many colours, light, holds the style well; ends can be sealed with hot water.
Some fibres itch or irritate the scalp; cannot be heat styled unless the maker says.
Human hair
Real hair, bought in bundles.
Looks and moves like natural hair; can be washed and styled with heat.
More costly; heavier; can tangle.
Yarn
Wool or acrylic thread, used for some braids and twists.
Soft; very light; cheap.
Can mat and hold lint; needs care when washing.
Blended hair
A mix of types.
Combines looks and costs.
Check the maker's advice.

ul: Start from the **style, length and colour** the client wants and how long she will keep it.
Choose a **weight** her own hair can hold. Heavy extensions on weak hair pull it out at the root. Lighter braids are kinder.
Match the colour to her hair or to the shade she has chosen. Show her the pack in daylight before you start.
Read the maker's instructions. Check the pack is clean and sealed.
Ask whether she has itched or reacted to extension hair before.

blocks.note: Some clients find synthetic braiding hair makes the scalp itch or sting. The fibre may have a coating that irritates. Rinse or soak the hair in cool water first (many stylists use a diluted vinegar soak, then rinse and dry fully), or use another type, as the instructor advises. If a client reacts badly, take the braids out and refer her to a doctor.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Item
What it is for
rows: Tail comb
Makes clean, straight partings. Hold it away from the face.
Wide-tooth comb and detangling brush
Detangle from the ends.
Sectioning clips
Hold back hair not yet braided.
Scissors
Trim extension ends and remove braids. Close after each use.
Applicator bottle and spray bottle
Spread diluted shampoo or water evenly.
Light gel, mousse or braiding cream
A small amount helps smooth the hair. Too much builds up, flakes and attracts dirt.
Hot water container, with a lid and a handle
To seal the ends of synthetic braids safely.
Hairdryer with a comb nozzle
Stretches natural hair. Use a heat protectant.
Rubber bands, elastic ties and beads (small, light)
Hold the ends and decorate if the client wants. Heavy beads can pull and hurt.

blocks.note: Extension hair and tools must never touch the floor. Put a clean towel on the trolley and keep hair in a closed container or its packet.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The consultation is a short, private talk before the service. You agree the style, check that the scalp and hair are fit for it, and explain the time, the care needed and the price. Do it at the chair, with the hair dry, in good light.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask what she wants
Look at and feel the scalp and hair
Check for contra-indications
Explain the style, time, price and care
Agree and record

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The style, size, length, pattern and colour
Show pictures so you both mean the same. Size decides how long the service takes and how much pull the hair takes.
The extension: type, weight, whether she has reacted before
Guides the choice and warns you of itching.
How long she wants to keep the style, and her lifestyle
Decides the style and the advice on washing and removal.
The last braiding: how long it was in, whether it hurt, any thinning or bumps
Shows whether her hair and edges have already been harmed.
Chemical services: a relaxer in the last weeks, colour, bleach
A scalp that is still sore from a relaxer cannot be braided. Weak chemically treated hair needs light braids.
Allergies, sensitive skin, headaches, health
To avoid products or positions that harm her.
Time and money
A full head of small braids can take many hours and cost more. Agree before you start.

ul: Part the hair in several places and look at the scalp under good light. Look at the **edges** (front hairline and temples) and the nape: they are the weakest part.
Feel the hair: check its length (it needs enough to hold a braid), its strength (does it stretch and spring back, or snap?), its density and its condition.
Look for flakes, redness, sores, cuts, bumps, bald or broken patches, and anything stuck to the hairs.

head: Finding
Contagious?
What you do
rows: Head lice or nits (small insects; eggs glued to hairs near the scalp)
Yes
Do not braid. Tell the client privately and kindly; suggest a pharmacist or doctor. Disinfect what she touched.
Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis): round, scaly patches, broken hairs or bald areas
Yes
Do not braid. Refer her to a doctor.
Impetigo: weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts
Yes
Do not braid. Refer her to a doctor.
Boils, pus spots or infected hair follicles (folliculitis)
Can spread
Do not braid over them. Refer her to a doctor.
Cuts, sores, scabs or recent surgery
No, but germs can enter
Do not braid over broken skin; wait until it heals.
Psoriasis or eczema (scaly or itchy patches)
No
If the skin is unbroken, use a light touch and loose braids. If broken or inflamed, do not braid.
Dandruff or dry scalp (flakes, no redness)
No
Carry on; advise on scalp care while the braids are in.
Thinning or bald patches at the edges, bumps, or a sore scalp (signs of traction alopecia)
No
Do not braid tightly over them. Suggest a rest, a looser style or a doctor.
Very weak, short or broken hair
No
Choose light braids or a different style; advise treatment first.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not tell a client she has a disease, and never try to treat an infection or infestation yourself. Describe what you saw, in private, say why the service cannot go ahead, advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist, and write it on the record card.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Parents of children often bring them for braids before school starts. If you find lice, tell the parent kindly and privately, never in front of other clients or the child's friends. Lice are no sign of a dirty home.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Well-prepared hair is clean, moisturised, detangled and stretched. It braids neatly with less pull.

flow: Check the scalp
Shampoo gently and condition
Detangle in sections from the ends
Rinse and blot
Apply a light leave-in
Stretch the hair
Section with a tail comb and clips

ul: **Shampoo** to remove dirt, oil and old product, then condition. (See the shampooing and conditioning unit for the method.)
**Detangle gently in sections,** starting at the ends and working up to the roots with your fingers and a wide-tooth comb. Never start at the roots: it pushes knots into tangles that tear the hair.
**Do not braid soaking wet hair.** It shrinks as it dries, so the braids get tighter. Braid damp or dry hair.

**Stretch** the hair so that it is easier to part and braid with less pulling. Methods: blow-drying on low to medium heat with a comb nozzle and a heat protectant, or banding or twisting the hair while it dries. Stretching does not make the hair longer; it only makes it easier to work.
Put on a **light** moisturiser or leave-in. Heavy creams make the braid slippery and build up under the braid.
Use the tail comb to make **clean, straight partings**. A crooked parting shows through the finished braid.
Make partings **even in size** so the style is balanced and the weight is shared evenly.
Clip away the hair you are not working on, so that it does not tangle.
Plan and agree the pattern of cornrows before you start. Work from the nape up, or as the plan says, and finish one section before you start the next.

blocks.note: Do not make a parting by pulling the comb hard through dry hair. It breaks the hair and tears the scalp. Wet the hair lightly or use a little product and work gently.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Part a clean, straight row with the tail comb; clip the rest of the hair away
Divide the hair at the front of the row into three equal strands
Cross the right strand **under** the middle strand, then the left strand under the new middle strand
Pick up a small, even amount of hair from the parting line only, adding it to the outer strand before it crosses
Keep the rows straight and the pieces you pick up the same size
Keep an even, firm, not tight tension and keep your hands close to the scalp
At the nape, carry on as a normal three-strand braid to the ends
Finish the end neatly, with a small elastic or by sealing it

ul: To keep the row straight, pick up hair **evenly and only from its own section**. Picking up from the next row makes it crooked.
The strands cross under so that the braid sits raised on the scalp.
Every row needs the same tension from front to back. A tight beginning gives a sore scalp and a loose end looks poor.
Check the first rows in the mirror. Fix any crooked rows at once, not at the end.
Start with a small amount of the client's own hair.
Add a thin piece of extension hair with the second or third cross, and again after a few more crosses.
Add a little at a time. Putting a thick pile of extension at the start makes the root heavy and tight.
Match the colour and keep the thickness of the row even as it moves back.

flow: Part the hair into sections and clip them; start at the nape
Make a square parting with the tail comb, the size you agreed
Divide the client's hair in the parting into three strands (or start the braid with a small amount of hair)
For box braids with extensions, add the extension hair evenly to each strand at the root, using the amount the plan says
For knotless braids, start the braid with the client's own hair and feed in the extension a little at a time
Braid down to the ends with even, firm, not tight tension
Finish and seal the end; check the base of the braid for pulling
Keep the partings even and take extra care at the hairline

ul: Use the same amount of extension in every braid, so they look and weigh the same.
The smaller the braid, the greater the pull on each hair and the longer the service. Small braids on fragile hair can break it.
Take extra care at the hairline and edges: the hair is fine there and breaks easily. Use smaller amounts, lighter extension and less tension.
Divide the section into two equal strands.
Wind them round each other in the same direction, with the same tension, keeping your hands close to the hair.
For a flat twist, add hair from the parting line as you go, like a cornrow.
Seal or roll the ends. If the client wants a twist-out, let the twists dry fully before you undo them.

For synthetic braids, one safe method is to dip the ends into hot water for a few seconds, away from the skin, then let them set. Check the maker's advice, because not all fibres seal this way. The container must be steady and away from the client.
A flame melts the ends, but it is a fire and burn risk. Do not use a flame near the client or her hair. Follow the Centre's rule.
For human hair or natural twists, secure the ends with a small elastic or curl them with a rod or a roller.
Trim any stray bits of extension with scissors, cutting away from the skin.
Check every braid for loose ends and loose roots.

blocks.note: Never seal braid ends over the client's head, neck or shoulders. Take the braid away from her skin, and keep hot water at a distance.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Traction alopecia** is hair loss caused by constant pulling on the hair. In braiding it happens at the edges, temples and nape, where the hair is fine and the pull is strongest. Early on the hair grows back. If the pulling continues for years, the follicle can be damaged for good. Prevention is your job.

ul: Braids that are too tight at the root.
Extensions that are too heavy for the client's own hair.
Very small braids on fine or fragile hair.
Keeping braids in too long, so that new growth pulls on the braid.
Repeated tight styles with no rest between them.
Tight ponytails, buns or beads on a braided head.

blocks.h: Signs that a braid is too tight

head: Sign
What it means
rows: Pain, burning or headache after braiding
Tension is too high. Loosen or redo.
Redness or swelling at the base of the braids
The skin is irritated by pulling.
Small bumps or pimples at the root (folliculitis)
The follicle is infected or inflamed.
Scalp pulled up into small peaks around the braid (tenting)
The braid pulls the scalp up. Redo it.
Thinning edges, short broken hair at the hairline
Traction is already damaging the hair.
The client cannot move her eyebrows or sleep comfortably
Style is too tight overall.

ul: Use **firm but not tight** tension. A braid should be secure, not painful.
Choose a braid size and extension weight the client's hair can hold.
Take extra care at the edges: smaller pieces, lighter extension, less tension, or leave a little hair out.
Ask the client during the service whether it feels comfortable, and check the base of each braid for tenting.
Do not put heavy beads on children's hair.
Advise a rest between styles and a limit on how long she keeps the braids.
If she says it hurts, **loosen or redo** those braids at once. Do not tell her it will ease in a week or to take a painkiller.

blocks.note: A child's hair is fine and her scalp is tender. Keep the tension low, the braids light and the partings larger. Tight edges, heavy extensions and beads can harm a child's hair for years.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: If a client comes back days after braiding with painful, pus-filled bumps on the scalp, loosen or remove the braids and refer her to a doctor. Do not put gel or oil over the bumps, and do not re-braid the area.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Tell the client how to care for her braids, and give the reason for each point.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Cleanse the scalp gently with diluted shampoo or a cleansing spray, rinse well and **dry fully**
A dirty scalp itches and flakes; damp braids smell and can grow mildew.
Use a light moisturiser or leave-in spray, not heavy oils, waxes or butters
Heavy products build up under braids.
Sleep in a satin or silk bonnet or on a satin pillowcase
Cotton soaks up moisture and rubs the hair and braids.
Do not tie braids up in tight buns or ponytails
It pulls on the roots and the edges.
Do not keep braids in too long (often 6 to 8 weeks at most)
Hair grows out and the braid pulls on it; build-up grows.
Come back if there is pain, itching, bumps or a bad smell
These are signs of tension, infection or mildew.
Rinse with fresh water after swimming or sea bathing, and dry the braids
Sea water and chlorine dry the hair; damp braids smell.

blocks.note: Humid Jamaican weather means braids can stay damp for hours. Teach the client to dry braids fully with a towel and a cool or low-heat dryer, not to leave them wet.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Explain to the client what to expect, including normal shedding
Wash and moisturise the braids first if the client wants
Cut the braid below the natural hair, never near the root
Unbraid gently from the end to the root
Use water or a leave-in to help remove tangles
Remove loose hair and build-up gently
Shampoo, deep condition and detangle from the ends
Check the scalp and edges and advise a rest

ul: **Never cut at the scalp or the root.** Scissors near the hair can cut the client's own hair.
Do not pull braids out quickly. Pulling breaks hair and hurts.

A lot of loose hair comes away when braids are taken out. This is normal: hair that shed naturally during the weeks was held in the braid. Many people shed roughly 50 to 100 hairs a day. It is not hair torn out, but tell the client what to expect.
Check the braids are neat, even, secure and comfortable.
Check that there are no loose ends and that the scalp is not red or sore.
Show the client the back with a hand mirror and ask whether she is happy.

flow: Sweep up hair and extension pieces and bin them
Clean, then disinfect combs, clips and tools
Empty and clean the hot water container
Put used towels, capes and neck strips in the closed laundry bin
Wipe surfaces and the trolley
Wash your hands

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name, contact details
07/11/2026, Tamika Stewart, Kingston
Scalp and hair findings
Fine texture, medium density, edges thin; no scalp problems
Style, size and extension
Knotless box braids, medium; synthetic, lightweight; 6 packs
Time taken and price
6 hours; JMD 12,000 (example only)
Reactions or problems
Mild itching, solved by rinsing the extension
Aftercare given
Cleanse the scalp weekly; satin bonnet; remove in 6 to 8 weeks
Stylist
A. Williams (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Prices are for you to agree with your salon. JMD amounts here are only examples. Always agree the price and the time with the client before you start.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: I can use scissors, hot water and sealing tools safely and give first aid for a scald.
I can clean and disinfect combs and clips, and say why cleaning comes first.
I can name the main braided styles and say which suits which client.
I can tell cornrows (cane rows), box braids, knotless braids and twists apart.
I can describe synthetic, human hair and yarn extensions and choose a weight that suits the client's hair.
I can deal with itching from synthetic hair.
I can carry out a consultation and check the scalp and edges.
I can recognise head lice, ringworm and impetigo, and say what to do.
I can prepare natural hair: detangle from the ends, stretch it and section it.
I can braid a straight, even cornrow with an underhand braid and firm tension.
I can feed extension hair into a cornrow little by little.
I can put in box braids with square partings and even tension.
I can seal the ends of braids safely.
I can explain traction alopecia, its causes and its signs.
I can recognise a braid that is too tight and loosen or redo it.
I can give aftercare advice with the reasons.
I can take braids out without damaging the hair.
I can clean up and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I add the extension hair a little at a time so that there is less pull on the root.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A flat braid made close to the scalp, picking up hair along a parting.
A braid in which the strands cross under the middle one, so it sits raised on the scalp.
A braid in which the strands cross over the middle one.
Adding extension hair a little at a time as the braid goes along.
A single braid from a square parting.
A box braid that starts with the client's own hair and has no knot at the root.
Two strands wound round each other.
A two-strand twist made flat on the scalp.
Hair or fibre added to the client's own hair to give length, fullness or colour.
Wool or acrylic thread sometimes used instead of hair.
The line made with a comb that divides one section of hair from another.
A comb with a long thin handle, used for partings.
The fine hair around the front hairline and temples.
How tightly the hair is pulled while braiding.
The scalp pulled into small peaks round a braid that is too tight.
Hair loss caused by constant pulling on the hair.
Inflamed or infected hair follicles, seen as bumps or pus spots.
Making curly or coily hair longer for working, for example with a dryer or by banding.
Curly hair becoming shorter as it dries.
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
Removing dirt, hair and product with detergent and water.
Killing most germs on clean tools with a chemical.
The client's record of her hair, the service, products, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: A client with thinning edges in Kingston
c1.text: Tamika Stewart, 22, comes to a salon in Kingston for waist-length, small knotless box braids. Her last braids stayed in for four months. Trainee Andre notices that her hair is fine, her edges are short and thin, and there are small red bumps along the hairline. Tamika says her scalp was sore for the first week of her last style and that she wants the new ones very tight 'so they last'.

c2.title: School braids in Old Harbour
c2.text: Mrs. Donna Gordon brings her daughter Keisha, aged 6, to a salon in Old Harbour for micro braids with plastic beads, to last until the end of the term. Keisha's hair is fine and short. Her mother asks the trainee, Shanique, to braid it very tightly so that it does not come loose at school.

c3.title: Cornrows at the training salon
c3.text: In the Centre's salon, trainee Ricardo is braiding feed-in cornrows on a practice head with natural hair. He adds a thick pile of extension hair at the start of each row, pulls tightly on the first few crosses, and picks up hair from the neighbouring row when a parting becomes thin. The rows start out straight but curve towards the end, and the root of each row looks raised and tight.

c4.title: A long service in Ocho Rios
c4.text: A salon in Ocho Rios is busy. Stylist Cheryl has been braiding for five hours without a break while the client, Mrs. Beverley Lewis, sits with her feet dangling and says her back and legs are stiff. Cheryl bends low over the client and has her stool at its lowest height. To seal the braid ends, she holds a pot of hot water over the client's shoulder and a pair of open scissors in her back pocket.

c5.title: Taking braids out in Mandeville
c5.text: Janice Reid, 27, from Mandeville has had box braids for four months. Her scalp itches, the braids smell musty and a lot of new growth shows. She wants them out and plans to cut each braid off at her scalp. She asks trainee Marlon why so much hair comes out when the braids are undone, and whether she should go straight into new braids the next day.

questions.q: Which sign at Tamika's hairline most strongly suggests that her last braids pulled too tightly?
o: Her hair is fine in texture
She wants braids that last
Short, thin edges and red bumps
She had braids for four months
questions.why: Thin, broken edges and red bumps at the root are signs of traction and inflamed follicles. Fine hair and long wear make damage more likely, but they are not signs of it on their own.

questions.q: How should Andre answer Tamika's request for very tight braids?
o: Agree, and make them as tight as her hair will take
Explain the risk to her edges, and braid firmly, not tightly
Braid tightly at the edges but loosely on the rest of the head
Agree, but leave the edges out of the first few braids
questions.why: Tight braids do not last longer and they cause pain, bumps and traction alopecia, especially on fine hair and weak edges. Explain why, and use firm but not tight tension.

questions.q: Which choice is best for Tamika's fine hair and thin edges?
o: Very small braids with heavy extension, so the hair is hidden
Medium knotless braids with light extension and extra care at the edges
Small box braids with a knot at the root, to hold the style in place
Tight cornrows along the hairline, with the braids on top
questions.why: Fragile hair and thin edges can take only light, low-tension styles. Larger, lighter knotless braids put less weight and pull on each hair. Small, heavy braids and tight cornrows at the hairline would add damage.

questions.q: While Andre braids, Tamika's scalp starts to pull up into small peaks around two braids. What should he do?
o: Redo those braids with less tension
Put gel on the braids to help them relax
Leave them, since they will loosen in a few days
Carry on, but make the next braids looser
questions.why: Scalp pulled into peaks (tenting) shows the braid is too tight. Loosen or redo the braids at once. Waiting, or applying products, does not solve the pull.

questions.q: What should Shanique say about Keisha's micro braids with beads?
o: They are fine, because small plastic beads weigh almost nothing
They are fine if the braids are tight, so that the beads stay put
Too heavy for her fine hair; offer light, loose cornrows or twists
They are fine, as long as they stay in only for the first week
questions.why: A child's hair is fine and her scalp tender. Very small braids and heavy beads put strong pull on each hair and can cause damage and pain. A light, low-tension style is the right advice.

questions.q: Mrs. Gordon says to braid tightly so that it stays in until the end of term. What is the best reply?
o: Agree, because children's hair needs a firm hold
Agree, and add extra gel to keep them from loosening
Agree, but put the tightest braids at the hairline
Explain that tight braids can hurt her and damage her hair
questions.why: Low tension keeps a child comfortable and protects her hair. A well-made light braid lasts without being tight. Gel does not fix a style that is already tight.

questions.q: How long is it sensible to advise Mrs. Gordon that braids should stay in?
o: A few weeks, often up to about 6 to 8 at most
Until the end of the term, however long that is
As long as they look neat, even if it is for months
Only a few days, since children's hair grows quickly
questions.why: New growth pulls on a braid as it grows, and build-up grows, so braids should not stay in too long. Six to eight weeks at most is a common guide for a child's style, and less is kinder.

questions.q: Why does Ricardo's feed-in cornrow feel tight and look raised at the root?
o: He used an underhand braid, which always sits raised
He added extension hair little by little
He added a thick pile of extension at the start
He picked up hair evenly from its own row
questions.why: A thick pile of extension at the start makes the root heavy and tight. Feed-in means adding a thin piece a little at a time, which gives less pull and a natural taper.

questions.q: Why do Ricardo's rows start straight but curve towards the end?
o: He is taking hair from the next row when a parting thins
He is using the tail comb at too steep an angle
He is keeping the strands the same size all the way
He is crossing the strands over the middle one
questions.why: To keep a row straight, pick up hair evenly and only from its own section. Hair taken from the neighbouring row pulls the braid off its line and thins the next row.

questions.q: Which braiding method makes a cornrow sit raised on the scalp?
o: Crossing the outer strands over the middle one
Crossing the outer strands under the middle one
Twisting two strands round each other
Tying a small knot at each section
questions.why: In a cornrow the strands cross under the middle one (underhand), so the braid is raised. Crossing over gives a French (overhand) braid that lies on top of the hair.

questions.q: When should Ricardo fix a crooked row?
o: At the end, when the whole head is done and he can see it
Straight away, by checking the first rows in the mirror
Only if the client complains about it
Never, since a small curve does not show in the finished style
questions.why: A crooked row is easiest to fix at the start. Check the first rows in the mirror as you go and redo any that go off line.

questions.q: What is the most important risk in the way Cheryl holds the hot water to seal the ends?
o: It will cool too fast and not seal the ends
It will change the colour of the extension hair
It could spill and scald Mrs. Lewis
It will make the braids itch
questions.why: Hot water over a seated client can scald her. Keep the container steady and away from her, dip the ends away from her skin, and never carry it past her.

questions.q: What should Cheryl do about the open scissors in her back pocket?
o: Keep them there, since she needs them quickly
Close them and keep them on the trolley or in a holder
Leave them open on Mrs. Lewis's lap for easy reach
Put them on the floor beside the stool
questions.why: Open scissors in a pocket can cut you or the client. Close them and keep them on the trolley or in a safe holder, and cut away from the skin.

questions.q: Which change would best help Mrs. Lewis's discomfort?
o: Ask her to hold still and finish as fast as possible
Turn off the lights to help her relax
Offer breaks, support her feet and check how she feels
Pull the braids tighter so that she has to move less
questions.why: A long service needs breaks, a good seat with the feet supported and regular checks. Rushing or pulling tighter makes things worse.

questions.q: Cheryl is bending low over Mrs. Lewis with her stool at its lowest. What should she change?
o: Stand on one leg to stay alert during the service
Hold her arms high above her head to see the partings
Bend lower over the client, to see the partings better
Raise the stool and change position often, with short breaks
questions.why: Stooping for hours causes back and neck pain. Adjust the height so that you can keep a straight back, change position, and take short breaks to stretch.

questions.q: Janice wants to cut each braid off at her scalp. What should Marlon do?
o: Let her, as it is the fastest way
Cut each braid near the scalp, but leave the new growth
Cut below her own hair, then unbraid gently
Pull each braid out from the root, starting at the nape
questions.why: Cutting at the scalp can cut her own hair. Cut below the natural hair, then take the braid out gently from the end to the root, using water or a leave-in to help with tangles.

questions.q: Why does so much hair come out when braids are undone?
o: The braids pulled the hair out at the roots
Hair that shed naturally was held in the braids
The hair is falling out from illness
The comb is breaking the hair
questions.why: Everyone sheds some hair each day. Braids hold that hair in, and it comes out together when the braids are taken down. It is normal, but tell the client what to expect.

questions.q: What should Marlon advise about new braids the next day?
o: Go straight into new braids to protect the hair from the weather
Wait a day or two, then braid again with tight braids
Rest the scalp first, with cleansing and deep conditioning
Put the new braids in at once, but make them smaller than before
questions.why: After months of braids, the scalp and hair need cleansing, deep conditioning and a rest. Going straight into another tight style keeps pulling on weak edges.

questions.q: A client says synthetic braiding hair always makes her scalp itch. What could the stylist do?
o: Use twice as much extension hair on each braid
Braid the extension in more tightly at the roots
Rinse the extension first or use another type of hair
Put the extension hair under a hot dryer
questions.why: Some synthetic fibres have a coating that irritates the scalp. Rinsing or soaking the hair first, or choosing another type, usually helps. More hair or more tension only makes it worse.

questions.q: A teenage client has weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts at her nape. What is the right action before braiding?
o: Clean the sores with a damp cloth, then braid over them
Braid the rest of her head and leave the nape loose
Braid gently, then ask her mother to treat the sores
Do not braid, and advise her privately to see a doctor
questions.why: Weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts are typical of impetigo, a contagious bacterial infection. Do not braid; do not name the disease to her, and refer her to a doctor. Disinfect everything she touched.
